# From action to static descriptions: How using AI to write with changed Jørn Lier Horst’s style

I had to laugh when I saw the title of the bestselling Norwegian novel that was just revealed to be heavily AI-assisted . It’s Jørn Lier Horst’s Den siste saken , or in English, The Last Case . So many of the AI-generated stories we analysed in this paper had titles that included the word “last”! As I’ll explain in this blog post, that’s not the only AI cliché in the book.

Unlike the datasets of stories we’ve been generating from simple prompts, The Last Case is an international bestseller by one of Norway’s most beloved crime authors, and it’s not 100% AI-generated, it’s just heavily AI-assisted. 73% AI according to Skrivera , a AI detector for Norwegian language that Aftenposten used last week to reveal that six of Horst’s recent books used AI . When I uploaded the text to Pangram it classified 34% of the novel as AI.

Horst has admitted to using AI, and defends his use of it . He explains that he uses ChatGPT for research and improving his text, but that he is the writer, and he stands by every word. I discuss some of his points in more detail below. Horst has received criticism from many other authors , but also support from some who argue that one might as well use AI if it’s efficient. And the readers of the book, which has already sold millions of copies internationally, may well not care either way . The book got good reviews, and is generally seen as a good book in its genre. But as I’ll show in this blog post, it does have some very characteristic AI tells. The most important, in my view, is the increase, compared to Horst’s previous novels, of passive and descriptive passages that do not move the action forward, and the use of typical AI clichés.

There are many reasons why AI-assisted novels might cause controversy, such as labour rights, copyright issues, the energy cost of using AI, damage to the reader’s trust in the author and publisher, and in Norway, the fact that the government heavily subsidises literature by buying copies of most published books for the country’s public libraries. Recently, Arts Council Norway released new guidelines saying that they would no longer buy AI-generated novels under this program, unless the AI was used for a specific aesthetic purpose. This might not matter much to Jørn Lier Horst, who sells plenty of books anyway.

None of these arguments speak to the quality or characteristics of the actual texts, though, which is what our research project, AI STORIES, is exploring. We have focused on fully AI-generated stories, where there are clear differences. A novel like Den siste saken is different: it is the product of an accomplished human author using AI in a way he feels is reasonable. So how much does this use of AI as a writing tool, if that is what it is, really affect the text itself?

In this blog post I’ll use data visualisation and examples of actual sentences to show differences between Horst’s new AI-assisted novel and two of the previous novels in the series that he wrote well before ChatGPT. In addition to the prevalance of some AI-typical clichés, the AI-assisted novel appears to have more descriptions of static settings, whereas earlier novels were told in a way that gave information about the setting through character actions.

## More nouns and adjectives, fewer pronouns and verbs

Several studies have found that AI-generated texts have more nouns and adjectives and fewer pronouns and verbs than human writing does (see, for instance, How LLMs Distort Human Writing ). When I ran a parts-of-speech analysis of Horst’s AI-assisted novel (so I could count how many nouns and verbs and so on it contains) I couldn’t see much of a difference to his earlier novels. But when I compared the sections of his novel that Pangram classifies as AI-generated to the sections classified as human, there is a very clear difference.

This visualisation shows differences between the AI and human-authored excerpts from Den siste saken and the averages from two of Horst’s earlier novels, Katharina-koden and Nattmannen . The baseline here – the horisontal line at 0% – is set to be the average occurance of adjectives, nouns, personal pronouns and verbs in the pre-AI novels. The blue bar is for excerpts from Den siste saken that are classified as human, and as you can see, they are pretty close to Horst’s earlier writing. However, the sentences classified as AI-generated by Pangram – the orange bars – are quite different. The AI sections of the novel have significantly more adjectives and nouns, and fewer personal pronouns and verbs, than his earlier writing. This is consistent with other research on AI-generated writing.

So then the question becomes whether this matters. Let’s look at some of the actual words and sentences in the novel.

## Humming / summing

One of the first sections Pangram classified as AI had a “humming” in it, which is, of course, a typical AI tell, so lets start there. Here’s the passage. I’ll use Google Translate for the translation to English – given that LLMs generally go via English we can safely assume that if the Norwegian text was AI generated it was heavily influenced by English anyway.

> Motoren surret jevnt, lyden lå lavt og konstant, en monoton vibrasjon i den tette stillheten. Wisting smalnet øynene og gransket området rundt bilen. Naustet sto mørkt og stille, ingen skygger beveget seg innenfor lyskjeglene. Han lot blikket gli langs bryggekanten, over den duppende båten og videre mot svaberget som omkranset stedet. ( The engine hummed steadily—a low, constant sound, a monotonous vibration within the profound silence. Wisting narrowed his eyes and scanned the area around the car. The boathouse stood dark and still; no shadows moved within the cones of light. He let his gaze travel along the edge of the pier, across the bobbing boat, and on toward the smooth, bare rock that encircled the site.)

Motoren surret jevnt, lyden lå lavt og konstant, en monoton vibrasjon i den tette stillheten. Wisting smalnet øynene og gransket området rundt bilen. Naustet sto mørkt og stille, ingen skygger beveget seg innenfor lyskjeglene. Han lot blikket gli langs bryggekanten, over den duppende båten og videre mot svaberget som omkranset stedet.

( The engine hummed steadily—a low, constant sound, a monotonous vibration within the profound silence. Wisting narrowed his eyes and scanned the area around the car. The boathouse stood dark and still; no shadows moved within the cones of light. He let his gaze travel along the edge of the pier, across the bobbing boat, and on toward the smooth, bare rock that encircled the site.)

Well, if you have read any AI-generated stories you’ll recognise the voice there. Humming and “low, constant sounds” are some of the most frequent tropes in AI-generated writing.

The most common Norwegian translation of “hum” is “summing”, and variants of this barely appear in Horst’s earlier novels. There is a lot of humming in Den siste saken , though. Just look at this! (I generated these wordtrees at Jason Davies’ website .)

Of course, humans can also write obsessively about humming. But there are only two hums ( summet ) in Katharina-koden (2017). This seems like a pretty signficant shift in word choice that certainly correlates with AI clichés.

## Quiet / stille

LLMs tend to love words like quiet, quietly, whispering, vanishing, humming, shimmering . A quick wordtree visualisation of how the word “stille” (quiet) is used in Katharina-koden and the new novel not only shows that the word is used signficantly more, but that the way it’s used has also changed.

In these wordtrees, each line is an occurrence in each of the novels. Notice the main uses in Den siste saken are passive descriptions of a setting rather than actions. The first wordtree shows how “stille” is used in the AI-assisted novel. Notice how the top examples are about something being quiet (“alt var stille”), a construction that Horst never uses in Katharina-koden from 2017. Quiet (“stille”) is used here to describe a static situation, not an action.

Keep reading down the list and you’ll see several other equivalent constructions:

- Wisting “sat quietly”

- “A quiet…”

- “she sat quietly”

- “she sat completely quietly…”

- “Lise shut her eyes and stayed lying quietly…”

- “Inside the compartment it was quiet…”

In Katharina-koden , shown in the next wordtree, the most common usage of “stille” ( quiet ) is “it became quiet”. “It became”: this describes something happening rather than a setting that just is . There is a transition from one state to another, from noise to quiet. This is a significant stylistic shift, from actions in Katharina-koden to static descriptions in Den siste saken . ## Binary oppositions

Stories don’t usually have the not X but Y formulations of non-fiction AI writing, but they do have binary oppositions that cancel each other out, both at the level of language and plot. We haven’t published on this yet in AI STORIES, but we’ve talked about it at presentations. I didn’t find many of these in Den siste saken , probably because Horst is a good writer and the novel obviously isn’t entirely AI-generated, but I have yet to read the whole novel carefully. I’ll admit I’ve been skimming and visualising to find examples and it would be good to do a more thorough close reading.

Here’s one example, though, of binary oppositions that cancel each other out at the level of language. This is from segment of Den siste saken that Pangram classified as AI-generated:

> Han utstrålte en naturlig selvsikkerhet , men det var noe ved ham som virket utilnærmelig, som om han bevisst holdt folk på avstand . He exuded a natural self-assurance, but there was something about him that seemed unapproachable, as if he were deliberately keeping people at a distance. Jørn Lier Horst: Den siste saken (2025) – text excerpt classified as AI-generated by Pangram

Han utstrålte en naturlig selvsikkerhet , men det var noe ved ham som virket utilnærmelig, som om han bevisst holdt folk på avstand .

He exuded a natural self-assurance, but there was something about him that seemed unapproachable, as if he were deliberately keeping people at a distance.

See how the LLM balances out the “natural self-assurance” (attracting people) with “unapproachable” and “keeping people at a distance” (repelling people)? A pull has to be balanced out with a push, like an equation where you have to keep the balance on either side of the equal sign.

At the plot level this is often evident in violence that causes no harm, as in Shy Girl , another AI-generated novel , where the villain shoots at the protagonist when she tries to escape, but does not hit her. We also see it when the story works up to a conflict or turning point that is instantly deflated or cancelled out. A good example is the turning point of “ Serpent in the Grove “, the short story that won an award before being found to be AI-generated. In “Serpent”, Sita’s husband plots to kill her, but when his plan succeeds and she falls into the well, a neighbour shows up out of nowhere to instantly rescue her. Here’s my plot diagram showing how this works in “Serpent in the Grove”. I wrote a bit more more about it in this blog post .

## The heavy weight of AI-generated stories

Air is always heavy, weighty in AI-generated texts, and so it is in Den siste saken . I checked Katharina-koden and sure, someone breathes heavily , and someone else’s face gets a heavy look, but there’s only one occurrance of heavy air, and it’s caused by the heat of an external harddrive, not by emotional weight. AI-generated stories tend to use the metaphor of heaviness and weight to signify emotional tension.
